newsitem.title: USA: Florida doctor acquitted of killing cancer patient.
newsitem.headline: Florida doctor acquitted of killing cancer patient.

text.p: A Florida jury Thursday acquitted a Colombian-born doctor who had been accused of killing a terminally ill patient with an overdose of pain medicine.
After five hours of deliberation, the jury found Ernesto Pinzon not guilty of first-degree murder. The family and friends of Pinzon erupted in joy when the verdict was announced.

As soon as the judge discharged him, Pinzon looked for his mother, who had sat in the first row behind him throughout the three-week trial. He embraced her and said: "I told you, what's true is true. I'm OK."
It was the first time in Florida a physician had been charged with first-degree murder in the care of a patient.
Pinzon later said the verdict was not a surprise. "I was really confident. I was not expecting surprises," he said.
Earlier Thursday, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that states have the right to prohibit doctor-assisted suicide.
Pinzon could have faced imprisonment for life if convicted of first-degree murder. The jury also considered lesser charges of second-degree murder and manslaughter.
In his closing argument, prosecutor John Aguero told jurors: "Nobody but God can figure out when you're going to die. Nobody but God has a right to take you."
Pinzon, 37, was accused of killing 70-year-old Rosario Gurrieri by injecting massive doses of morphine, followed by potassium chloride, a drug often used in executions by injection.

Gurrieri suffered from lung cancer that had spread into his spine and liver and other vital organs. His personal physician had given him about two days to live when Pinzon began to treat him in October at a Highlands County hospital.
Pinzon testified he was only trying to relieve Gurrieri's pain and had not tried to kill him. He contended that the patient died of his illness.
The case hinged on the testimony of a medical examiner, whose expertise was cast in doubt by a former employer. The examiner testified that Gurrieri died of morphine poisoning.
Defence lawyer Bill Fletcher called that "an invalid opinion based on medical ignorance," adding: "Patients are undermedicated because doctors are afraid to treat pain, and you can see why."
Gurrieri died surrounded by grieving relatives who had asked Pinzon to ease his suffering by injecting enough pain-killers to put him in a coma.

Aguero, the prosecutor, urged jurors to put aside their sympathy for Pinzon and his patient. "If this killing is merciful, it's murder. If this killing is compassionate, it's murder. The only way this death isn't murder is if the drugs didn't shorten or end his life," Aguero said.
